claims.claim: Campaign cutscenes feature a narrator and documentary-style historical footage rather than placing the player directly into the historical events.

citations.review_text:
Have well over 200 hours through game pass. Decided to finally buy it on steam while on sale. 

This is a fantastic game, with a great campaign. If you enjoy RTS games and history, you will like this, as they use real footage of historical sites intertwined with the campaign. 

You will advance through easy AI to hard pretty quickly once you get the hang of things and the difficulty is a lot of fun.

The gameplay itself is fine the campaigns suck and the narrator lacks emotion. The campaign doesn't make you feel like you're the one in charge at all, it just has a narrator talking down to you over and over again. There's no character interaction at all. If you're intending to play for the campaign like you would with AoE2 and AoE3, prepare to be disappointed.

Immersion completely ruined by the game being depicted as a "history lesson". Cars and modern-day technology are all over the place in the cutscenes, and the actual battles are just sillhouettes of ghost-warriors while the narrator talks to you as if she's a History teacher telling you about "what happened here 1000 years ago". I really hate it. Age of Empires 2 depicted the cutscenes as YOU BEING THERE IN THE MOMENT, whether you were a warrior or one of Saladin's followers or whatever. And if you wanted the full history lesson, there was a section for that hidden away in the menus. Turning your video game into a History Lecture sucks!

tl;dr  the stylistic choices kill the immersion

claims.claim: Reviewers state that the single-player mode lacks a pause feature to issue orders during matches.

citations.review_text:
Gameplay: 1 out of 10
Campaigns: Totally Sucks

I play Age of Empires IV exclusively against the AI. I have no interest in competitive multiplayer, ranked matches, or esports. For me, this game is a way to relax after work, enjoy a peaceful evening, think through my strategies, and simply have fun. That's why the lack of a proper pause feature in single-player is one of the most baffling and frustrating design decisions in the game.

I've never understood why, in a match where there are no human opponents, I can't pause the game and calmly issue orders. The AI won't get upset, it won't gain an unfair advantage, and it certainly won't mind waiting. I'm playing alone, so the only person's experience affected by this decision is mine.

Real-time strategy games involve an incredible amount of multitasking. You have to manage your economy, train villagers, produce military units, scout the map, defend multiple fronts, use unit abilities, expand your base, and constantly react to enemy attacks. As the match progresses, the workload increases dramatically. Sometimes you need to make several important decisions at the same time, and without the ability to pause, what should be an enjoyable strategy game turns into unnecessary stress.

I want to win because I made better strategic decisions, not because I can click faster than everyone else. Strategy games have always been about planning, decision-making, and tactical thinking. Without a pause feature, many interesting strategies become impractical simply because there's no time to execute them properly. Instead of thinking ahead, you're forced to rush every decision.

There are also everyday situations that every player experiences. Someone rings the doorbell. Your phone starts ringing. A family member needs your attention. You want to grab a drink or simply take a short break. In almost every single-player game, you just press Pause and continue when you're ready. In Age of Empires IV, however, you're forced to either let …

The game isn't fun unless you're a sweaty. Don't bother if you just want some casual fun. The bones are there but AOE 4 has none of the charm that AOE 2 had. It's too fast even on the lower difficulties. Gameplay has reduced down to nothing but spreadsheet optimization and rote learning exact sequences of what to click and when. There's no time to think, there's no time to explore, there's no time to admire anything, there's no time to experiment. It's just click click quick! quick!

Otherwise there's plenty of new features like game modes and challenges, stuff to unlock and achievements etc. The game has shifted towards a live service model with challenges and whatnot that cycle in and out, leaderboards and cosmetics etc.

Get it if you're a competitive AOE geek and want to get sweaty with PvP. Don't bother if you're casual AOE player who just wants to relax, build magnificent empires, and beat up the AI.

claims.claim: Reviewers mention that single-player campaigns include documentary-style videos between missions.

citations.review_text:
Every civilization feels like learning a completely different game. One day you're raining arrows as the English, the next you're relocating your entire civilization as the Mongols. Winning isn't just about having the biggest army—it's about planning ahead, adapting to your opponent, and staying calm when everything is falling apart.

The campaigns deserve more praise than they get. They don't just throw history at you—they make you feel like you're part of it. The documentary-style videos between missions are incredibly well made and made me appreciate the real events behind the battles.

What surprised me most was the balance between accessibility and depth. It's easy enough for newcomers to enjoy, yet deep enough that even after hundreds of hours, you're still learning new strategies, build orders, and counters. Every defeat feels like a lesson instead of wasted time.

The sound design is phenomenal. Hearing armies clash, castles collapse, and the music evolve as you advance through the ages creates an atmosphere few strategy games can match.

Is it perfect? No. Every RTS has balance patches and occasional frustrations. But when a match ends after an intense hour-long battle where both players gave everything they had, you remember why this series has remained legendary for decades.

If you enjoy strategy, history, or simply games that reward thinking instead of button mashing, Age of Empires IV is an easy recommendation.

Age of Empires IV is a great reminder that classic real-time strategy games still have a place in modern gaming.

The game keeps the core formula that made the series legendary: gather resources, build your civilization, develop your economy, and lead your army to victory. Every match feels like a new challenge where strategy and decision-making matter more than simply having a fast reaction time.

The attention to historical details is one of the strongest parts of the game. Each civilization feels unique, with different units, technologies, and playstyles. Learning their strengths and weaknesses makes every battle more interesting.

The campaigns are also impressive, combining gameplay with documentary-style storytelling. They make history feel more alive and help you understand the conflicts behind each civilization.

Of course, it is not perfect. Some players may find the learning curve challenging, and the pace can feel slow if you are used to faster modern strategy games. But that depth is exactly what makes Age of Empires special.

Age of Empires IV successfully brings a legendary franchise into the modern era without forgetting its roots. A must-play for strategy fans and anyone who enjoys building an empire from nothing.

Wololo forever.

claims.claim: Reviewers note that the base game has a limited selection of content without purchasing expensive downloadable content.

citations.review_text: Its mostly aimed at multiplayer and there's a lot of expensive dlc, base game is pretty limited without it.

I've got a lot of love for this game and this franchise. I can't support filling it with paywalls though, so I will not recommend it. Two of the campaigns and 13 of the playable civilizations are locked behind DLC. That's in a game that isn't super content heavy. Base game has 4 campaigns and 10 playable civilizations. They pulled the same thing years ago with AoE2 and it was just as asinine then as it is now.  I can't help but think Xbox was the driving force on doubling down on the DLC. They do this blatantly in the face of a thinning player base. An incredible franchise like this should not be treated this way.
Also, totally off topic but have you guys tried that AoE mobile game? ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ yikes.

claims.claim: Reviewers report that civilisations and campaigns are locked behind paid downloadable content.

citations.review_text:
Excellent game, and probably the RTS I'd recommend to someone starting the genre, as the design is more slow-paced and forgiving than say, starcraft 2, you can scout quite easily to understand what is going on, and the system of rock-paper-scissor between base units is pretty intuitive (pikemen are good vs cav, cav is good vs archers, archer weak vs heavily armored units...etc).

Outside of the appeal to casual players, I'd say AOE4's main strengths are 1)it's top tier sound design 2)it strikes a good balance of assymetry between factions 3) It does have a strong depth of decision-making that make it a true strategy game.

(Also not the most relevant for me or most steam users but the adaptation to console was very well done, and the game is much more suited for that than most rts)


The game was released in 2021 probably 6-8 months too early (some executives likely wanted it out for christmas sales at all cost), lacking key features, with a limited amount of civs and regular bugs, which probably did a lot of damage to the true success it should have known. 

But as times went on the game kept being slowly polished, progressively got nearly all asked features (now lacking only resume-from-replay), managed to satisfactingly rework siege and naval warfare, added many civs and some solo content through dlcs (although these are not mandatory to enjoy the game and most of its content) and the game only keep getting better and better.

Don't hesitate to jump in or ask the community for help and questions ;)

[h2] Pros: [/h2] 
[h3] 1. The campaign is actually interesting [/h3]
The campaigns do a good job of combining gameplay with history. You get historical information, short videos and extra context as you play, so you can actually learn something while playing the game. It doesn't feel like you're just reading a history book, either.

[h3] 2. The civilizations feel genuinely different [/h3]
This is probably the biggest improvement compared to previous AoE games.
In the older games, the main difference between civilizations was usually the tech tree, a couple of unique units and some small bonuses. In AoE4, the civilizations feel much more distinct. They have their own mechanics, playstyles and overall feeling.
This is the first game in the series where I actually find choosing a civilization interesting in itself, rather than just picking one because I like its units or bonuses.

[h3]3. Looks good and runs well [/h3]
The game looks good and, at least on my PC, runs smoothly. I haven't had any major performance issues, so the optimization seems pretty solid.

[h3]4. A lot of content[/h3]
Even if you don't play ranked multiplayer, the campaigns and the different civilizations can give you tens of hours of enjoyable gameplay. There is quite a lot to do before the game starts feeling repetitive.

[h2] Cons:[/h2] 
[h3]1. Unit micro can feel a bit clunky[/h3]
Controlling units sometimes feels a little bit awkward. It's not as smooth as StarCraft II, for example, and occasionally managing individual units or groups of units can feel a bit clunky.
Not a dealbreaker, but definitely something that could be improved.

[h3]2. Games can take a long time[/h3]
Obviously, this depends on your playstyle, the map and the number of players, but even a single game can take quite a while.
Sometimes I would like to play a shorter game, so I think some kind of faster game mode would be a nice add…

Excellent game, and probably the RTS I'd recommend to someone starting the genre, as the design is more slow-paced and forgiving than say, starcraft 2, you can scout quite easily to understand what is going on, and the system of rock-paper-scissor between base units is pretty intuitive (pikemen are good vs cav, cav is good vs archers, archer weak vs heavily armored units...etc).

Outside of the appeal to casual players, I'd say AOE4's main strengths are 1)it's top tier sound design 2)it strikes a good balance of assymetry between factions 3) It does have a strong depth of decision-making that make it a true strategy game.

(Also not the most relevant for me or most steam users but the adaptation to console was very well done, and the game is much more suited for that than most rts)


The game was released in 2021 probably 6-8 months too early (some executives likely wanted it out for christmas sales at all cost), lacking key features, with a limited amount of civs and regular bugs, which probably did a lot of damage to the true success it should have known. 

But as times went on the game kept being slowly polished, progressively got nearly all asked features (now lacking only resume-from-replay), managed to satisfactingly rework siege and naval warfare, added many civs and some solo content through dlcs (although these are not mandatory to enjoy the game and most of its content) and the game only keep getting better and better.

Don't hesitate to jump in or ask the community for help and questions ;)
